cards.heading: Testing isn't about coverage
cards.hook: Testing is about confidence — shipping code knowing it works, and that future changes won't silently break it.

cards.heading: The pyramid, bottom to top
cards.hook: Many fast unit tests at the base, fewer integration tests in the middle, and a handful of slow E2E tests at the top.
cards.body: Inverting that ratio — lots of E2E, few unit tests — is the most common testing mistake teams make.

cards.heading: What a unit test actually covers
cards.hook: A unit test isolates a single function or class with every dependency mocked, running in milliseconds.
cards.body: Hundreds or thousands of them can live in a healthy codebase without slowing anyone down.

cards.heading: What integration tests catch that unit tests can't
cards.hook: Integration tests use the real database, Redis, or file system — slower, but they catch the contract bugs between layers that mocks paper over.

cards.heading: E2E tests are expensive on purpose
cards.hook: End-to-end tests exercise the whole system from the outside, HTTP request to DB to HTTP response.
cards.body: Reserve them for a few dozen critical paths like checkout and login, not everything.

cards.heading: Test behavior, not implementation
cards.hook: A test that spies on a private method breaks on every refactor — assert on the observable result instead, and it survives any internal rewrite.

cards.heading: Test the contract, not the internals
cards.hook: expect(user._data.profile.name) breaks the moment that internal shape changes — expect(user.getName()) doesn't care how the data is stored.

cards.heading: Not everything deserves a test
cards.hook: Business logic, edge cases, and error paths are worth testing — simple getters, framework code, and one-line wrappers mostly aren't.

cards.heading: Every test is Arrange, Act, Assert
cards.hook: Set up the scenario, call the thing under test, verify the outcome — keep the three phases visually separated.
cards.body: A 50-line Arrange section is a sign the test is covering too much at once.

cards.heading: A test name is documentation
cards.hook: test('handles edge case') tells you nothing when it fails — test('throws NotFoundError when order does not exist') tells you exactly what broke.

cards.heading: The naming pattern that scales
cards.hook: [action/condition] [expected result] as the template means a failing test literally explains itself in the output.
cards.code: OrderService > placeOrder > throws InsufficientInventoryError when stock is 0

cards.heading: Tests must not depend on each other
cards.hook: Every test should start from a clean state and be runnable in any order.

cards.heading: Cleaning up after integration tests
cards.hook: beforeAll runs migrations once, beforeEach seeds fresh data, afterEach truncates tables.
cards.body: Each test gets a clean slate without paying the migration cost every single time.

cards.heading: Stub, mock, spy, fake — four different tools
cards.hook: A stub returns canned data, a mock also verifies it was called correctly, a spy wraps a real implementation and just watches, and a fake is a simplified-but-working version for when the real thing is too slow.

cards.heading: When to reach for which double
cards.hook: Need a dependency to return specific data? Stub. Need to verify it was called right? Mock. Watching a real implementation run? Spy. The real thing is a slow DB or external API? Fake.

cards.heading: FIRST: what makes a test good
cards.hook: Fast, Isolated, Repeatable, Self-checking, Timely — a test missing any one of these five quietly stops getting trusted, then stops getting run.

cards.heading: Testing implementation details breaks on every refactor
cards.hook: expect(service._internalState).toBe('ready') couples the test to code that has no business being tested — it'll break the next time someone renames a private field, for no real reason.

cards.heading: One test, one behavior
cards.hook: A test with ten assertions tells you something failed but not which.
cards.body: Splitting it into one assertion per test turns a vague red into an exact diagnosis.

cards.heading: Testing the mechanism instead of the outcome
cards.hook: expect(spy).toHaveBeenCalled() on an Axios call checks that a library was invoked, not that the behavior is right — assert on the actual transaction ID or status instead.

cards.heading: A skipped test is a silent liability
cards.hook: Marking a failing test test.skip instead of fixing it quietly erases the safety net it used to provide.

cards.heading: Coverage is a metric, not a goal
cards.hook: 100% coverage can still ship bugs — coverage only proves code ran during a test, never that the test actually checked anything meaningful.

cards.heading: Where to actually aim for high coverage
cards.hook: Business logic, utility functions, and error-handling paths deserve high coverage — boilerplate, generated code, and simple getters don't need the same bar.

cards.heading: Red, Green, Refactor
cards.hook: Write a failing test first, write just enough code to pass it, then refactor with the safety net already in place.
cards.body: TDD forces you to design the interface before the implementation exists.

cards.heading: Where TDD earns its keep
cards.hook: Business logic, algorithms, and utility functions are where TDD shines — exploratory UI work and unknown domains are where it gets in the way.

cards.heading: Each layer trades speed for confidence
cards.hook: Unit tests run in milliseconds but only prove the logic is right in isolation; E2E tests are slow and brittle but prove the whole system actually works together.
cards.body: Neither layer replaces the other — that's exactly why the pyramid has three levels.

cards.heading: A test suite nobody trusts gets ignored, not fixed
cards.hook: Once a team starts re-running a flaky test until it passes, every red in that suite stops meaning anything.
cards.body: Fixing the flakiness is more urgent than it feels in the moment.

cards.heading: Wiring up Jest
cards.hook: testEnvironment: node plus a testMatch pattern is most of what Jest needs to find and run your tests.
cards.body: ES modules need an extra babel-jest preset layered on top.

cards.heading: testMatch decides what counts as a test file
cards.hook: A pattern like **/*.test.js is what keeps Jest from accidentally trying to run your source files or fixtures as test suites.

cards.heading: Watch mode speeds up the feedback loop
cards.hook: jest --watch reruns only the tests affected by your latest change, turning the suite into a live feedback loop instead of a full run every save.

cards.heading: toBe vs toEqual
cards.hook: toBe checks strict equality for primitives — toEqual does a deep comparison, which is what you actually want for objects and arrays.

cards.heading: The assertion you forget: toBeCloseTo
cards.hook: Floating point math makes toBe(0.3) fail unpredictably — toBeCloseTo(0.3, 5) compares within a tolerance instead of expecting exact binary equality.

cards.heading: Partial matches without listing every field
cards.hook: toMatchObject checks that an object contains the given fields with the given values, ignoring everything else.

cards.heading: Asserting on thrown errors
cards.hook: expect(() => fn()).toThrow(ValidationError) checks the error type, not just that something was thrown — being specific here catches the wrong kind of failure.

cards.heading: Testing promises cleanly
cards.hook: await expect(promise).resolves.toBe(...) and .rejects.toThrow(...) read cleaner than wrapping everything in try/catch.

cards.heading: jest.mock replaces a whole module
cards.hook: jest.mock('./emailService.js') swaps every export for a jest.fn() automatically — then you control exactly what each call returns.

cards.heading: Mocking just the methods you need
cards.hook: A factory passed to jest.mock lets you mock only specific exports instead of silently stubbing every function in the module.

cards.heading: Classes get auto-mocked too
cards.hook: jest.mock('./PaymentGateway.js') turns every method on that class into a jest.fn() automatically — set its return value directly on the prototype.

cards.heading: A stub is often a one-liner
cards.hook: jest.fn().mockResolvedValue(...) with no class and no implementation is often all a dependency needs to be for a unit test.

cards.heading: DI makes mocking unnecessary
cards.hook: A class that accepts its dependencies through the constructor can be tested with plain fake objects — no jest.mock() magic required at all.

cards.heading: beforeEach vs beforeAll
cards.hook: beforeAll runs once for the whole describe block — good for expensive setup like DB connections. beforeEach runs before every single test — good for resetting state so tests can't leak into each other.

cards.heading: Clear your mocks between tests
cards.hook: jest.clearAllMocks() in beforeEach resets call counts so a mock called in test one doesn't silently inflate the assertions in test two.

cards.heading: Snapshot tests catch unexpected changes
cards.hook: toMatchSnapshot() saves a function's output the first time and fails the test if it ever changes.
cards.body: Ideal for HTML templates and serialization, risky for anything with a timestamp.

cards.heading: Keeping dynamic data out of snapshots
cards.hook: expect.any(String) and expect.any(Date) let a snapshot-style assertion ignore fields that are expected to change on every run, like generated IDs.

cards.heading: The happy path is the easy 10%
cards.hook: Error paths are where bugs actually hide — testing that a service rolls back an order when payment fails matters more than testing that it succeeds.

cards.heading: Verify what didn't happen, not just what did
cards.hook: expect(mockPayment.charge).not.toHaveBeenCalled() after a failed inventory check proves the system didn't charge a card for stock it didn't have.
cards.body: A subtler and more important assertion than just checking the error message.

cards.heading: test.each kills repetitive test code
cards.hook: One test.each table replaces five nearly-identical test blocks, and adding a new case is a one-line row instead of a copy-pasted function.

cards.heading: Constructor injection is the cheapest testability win
cards.hook: A class built as new OrderService({orderRepo, emailService, paymentService}) can be tested with four plain objects — no module mocking, no magic.

cards.heading: One behavior, one test, even in a real service
cards.hook: OrderService.placeOrder's test cases each check exactly one outcome — order created, marked PAID, email sent, stock enforced.
cards.body: So a failure immediately says which specific behavior broke, not just that something did.

cards.heading: Unit tests check the logic, integration tests check the wiring
cards.hook: A mocked unit test can pass even when your SQL has a typo, your schema doesn't match, or a foreign key blocks the insert — only a real database catches that.

cards.heading: Pick the layer, not just 'integration'
cards.hook: Repository-to-DB, service-to-Redis, HTTP-to-service — each boundary needs its own integration tests, because each one breaks in a different way.

cards.heading: Use a real test database, not a mock
cards.hook: A dedicated test database with real migrations run against it proves your queries, constraints, and indexes actually work — a mock can't catch a missing foreign key.

cards.heading: Truncate, don't recreate, between tests
cards.hook: TRUNCATE TABLE orders RESTART IDENTITY CASCADE in afterEach resets the table to empty without the cost of dropping and recreating it for every test.

cards.heading: Postgres returns numbers as strings — test for it
cards.hook: A NUMERIC column comes back from pg as a string, not a JS number.
cards.body: A test asserting total === 500 instead of '500' passes locally and fails against the real driver.

cards.heading: Supertest hits your real app without binding a port
cards.hook: Supertest starts your actual Express app in-process and fires real HTTP requests at it — testing routing, middleware, and response shape with no live server to manage.

cards.heading: Test the failure responses too
cards.hook: A 400 on an empty items array and a 401 on a missing Authorization header are just as much the contract as the 201 on success.
cards.body: They're exactly what a mocked unit test would never catch.

cards.heading: A Location header is part of the contract too
cards.hook: A 201 response that includes Location: /orders/42 lets a client immediately fetch the created resource — testing for its presence catches a regression a status-code-only check would miss.

cards.heading: Seed data directly, then act through HTTP
cards.hook: Inserting an order straight into Postgres and then hitting GET /orders/:id through the real HTTP layer isolates exactly what's under test.
cards.body: It tests only the read path, without re-testing the write path in the same case.

cards.heading: Don't mock auth in integration tests
cards.hook: Generating a real signed JWT and sending it through the real middleware is what actually proves your authentication and role checks work.

cards.heading: Role-based access needs its own test
cards.hook: A non-admin token hitting an admin-only route should return 403 — skip that test and a broken permission check ships silently.

cards.heading: Three ways to isolate integration tests
cards.hook: A shared test database with truncation between tests is simplest but can't run in parallel; wrapping each test in a transaction and rolling it back is fast but needs an injectable client; a separate database per test file is fully parallel-safe but more setup.

cards.heading: Transaction rollback is the fast option
cards.hook: BEGIN before the test, ROLLBACK after — no truncation, no cleanup queries, and the next test starts from an identical clean slate every time.

cards.heading: Flush, don't guess, between cache tests
cards.hook: client.flushDb() in afterEach clears every key so a cache test can't accidentally pass because a previous test left the right value behind.

cards.heading: TTL expiry is worth an explicit test
cards.hook: Setting a 1-second TTL and then actually waiting past it is the only way to prove cache invalidation logic works, not just that set and get round-trip correctly.

cards.heading: A seed helper beats repeating setup
cards.hook: seedUser() and seedOrder() helpers with sensible defaults let every test spin up exactly the data it needs in one line.

cards.heading: Keep unit and integration tests in separate directories
cards.hook: Fast unit tests run on every save; slower integration tests run in CI with --runInBand so they don't fight each other over the same test database.

cards.heading: A decision table beats a rule of thumb
cards.hook: Discount math is a unit test. SQL returning correct rows is an integration test. Can't-ship-an-unpaid-order needs both.
cards.body: Matching test type to what could actually break is the real skill, not a blanket rule.

cards.heading: Separating unit and integration test scripts
cards.hook: npm test runs only src/**/*.test.js fast on every save; npm run test:integration runs the slower suite against real infrastructure separately.

cards.heading: The slow degradation nobody notices
cards.hook: An API can look fine at 100 users, creep to 2 seconds at 1,000, and hit 10 seconds at 5,000.
cards.body: Because the growth is gradual, nobody notices until connections exhaust completely.

cards.heading: Why k6 over JMeter or Locust
cards.hook: k6 scripts are plain JavaScript, run from the command line with no GUI, and need no Python — which is exactly what fits cleanly into a Node.js team's CI/CD pipeline.

cards.heading: A virtual user is just a loop
cards.hook: vus: 10 and duration: '30s' means 10 simulated users each repeatedly running your script for 30 seconds.

cards.heading: check() is k6's assertion
cards.hook: check(response, {...}) doesn't fail the test run the way a thrown error would — it just records a pass/fail rate you read in the summary.

cards.heading: http_req_duration is the number that matters most
cards.hook: avg under 500ms is the common bar for a good user experience.
cards.body: But watch the gap between avg and p(95) — a big one means most users are fine while a meaningful slice are having a bad time.

cards.heading: p95 and p99 catch what averages hide
cards.hook: An average of 250ms can still have a p99 of 2 seconds — the 99th percentile tells you how bad the worst 1% of requests get, which the average silently erases.

cards.heading: http_req_failed is your error budget in one number
cards.hook: 0% failed is the target — anything above it means real requests are erroring under load, not just running slow.

cards.heading: Smoke test: the one-user sanity check
cards.hook: A smoke test runs with a single virtual user for a minute before anything heavier — its only job is confirming the system works at all.
cards.body: Cheap enough to run on every CI build.

cards.heading: Load test: your actual expected traffic
cards.hook: Ramp up to the number of users you really expect, hold steady, ramp down.

cards.heading: Stress test: finding where it actually breaks
cards.hook: Step the load up in stages — 100, 200, 300 users — and watch exactly which stage response time and error rate start climbing.
cards.body: That's your real breaking point, not a guess.

cards.heading: Spike test: can you survive a sudden flood
cards.hook: Jumping from 10 to 200 users in under a minute simulates a marketing email landing in 50,000 inboxes at once.
cards.body: The real question isn't just whether it degrades — it's whether it recovers after.

cards.heading: Soak test: the one that finds memory leaks
cards.hook: Running steady load for three hours instead of five minutes is what surfaces a memory leak.
cards.body: Response time creeping from 250ms to 5 seconds over hours is invisible in a short test.

cards.heading: A real user doesn't hammer the API nonstop
cards.hook: sleep(Math.random() * 3 + 2) between requests models actual think time — a script with no sleep at all tests a traffic pattern that will never really happen.

cards.heading: group() breaks a flow into named stages
cards.hook: Wrapping browse, add-to-cart, and checkout in group() blocks with different tags lets you set a stricter threshold on checkout than on browsing.
cards.body: Results come back broken down per step, not just as one blended average.

cards.heading: A login-then-act flow needs the token passed forward
cards.hook: Logging in, pulling the token out of the response, then using it as a Bearer header on the next request is what actually exercises the authenticated path, not just the login endpoint.

cards.heading: SharedArray loads test data once, not once per VU
cards.hook: Wrapping an array of test users in SharedArray means it's loaded into memory a single time and shared across every virtual user, instead of duplicated per VU.

cards.heading: Trend and Counter track what k6 doesn't by default
cards.hook: A custom Trend metric can measure just your checkout step's duration specifically, separate from the blended average across every endpoint the test hits.

cards.heading: Response time degradation has a short list of usual suspects
cards.hook: Database not scaling, no caching layer, synchronous code blocking the event loop, or CPU-bound work on the main thread — roughly in that order of likelihood.

cards.heading: 429 errors under load might be working as intended
cards.hook: Seeing rate-limit errors climb as load increases isn't necessarily a bug — it can be exactly the protection doing its job.
cards.body: The real decision is whether the limit itself needs raising.

cards.heading: Connection pool exhaustion looks like random failures
cards.hook: 0% errors at 50 users and 30% 'too many connections' errors at 100 is a pool sized too small for the concurrency, not a code bug.

cards.heading: Start small, then escalate
cards.hook: Smoke test with 1 user, then 10, then your real expected load, then a stress test to find the ceiling.
cards.body: Jumping straight to a stress test burns time chasing failures a smoke test would have caught in seconds.

cards.heading: Never load test production without explicit approval
cards.hook: A load test is, by design, trying to overwhelm a system — running one against production without sign-off is indistinguishable from an accidental denial-of-service.

cards.heading: Document your baseline so regressions are visible
cards.hook: A written baseline — p95 response time, error rate, throughput, on a specific infrastructure — turns 'feels slower' into 'p95 went from 450ms to 900ms since last quarter'.

cards.heading: Fail the build on a threshold breach, not just a crash
cards.hook: thresholds in k6 options make the test process exit non-zero when p(95) or error rate crosses your line.
cards.body: That's what actually blocks a bad deploy in CI instead of just producing a report nobody reads.

cards.heading: Run the smoke test on every deploy, the stress test monthly
cards.hook: A smoke test is cheap enough for every single CI run; a 3-hour soak test only makes sense before a major release.
cards.body: Matching test type to cadence is what keeps the pipeline fast.
